title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description: Find the smallest element of a sorted list that was rotated at an unknown point, in O(log n).
statement:
A list of **distinct** integers sorted in ascending order was rotated at an unknown point: some elements from the front were moved to the back, keeping their order. For example `[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7]` can become `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`. Return the smallest element of the rotated list `nums`.

- `nums` is never empty, and it may not be rotated at all.
- Return the value, not its index.
- Aim for **O(log n)**. The last tests pass a sequence of a billion numbers that supports only `len(nums)` and `nums[i]` and count how many elements you look at, so scanning or copying it will not work.

**Examples**

```python
find_min([3, 4, 5, 1, 2])          # 1
find_min([4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2])    # 0
find_min([11, 13, 15, 17])         # 11, the list is not rotated
```
hints: The minimum is the one element smaller than the element before it, the point where the rotation drops. Can you tell which side of the middle that point is on?
Compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[hi]`. If it is larger, the drop is to the right of `mid`; otherwise the minimum is at `mid` or to its left.
`mid` itself might be the minimum, so do not skip it: set `hi = mid` (not `mid - 1`) and loop while `lo < hi`. When the loop ends, `lo == hi` is the position of the minimum.
explanation:
**The idea.** In a rotated sorted list the minimum is the "drop": the one element that is smaller than the element before it (or the first element, if the list was not rotated). Compare the middle with the **last** element. If `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`, the drop lies to the right of `mid`, so the minimum is in `mid + 1..hi`. Otherwise `mid..hi` is in order, so the minimum is at `mid` or to its left. Each step discards half the range.

**Why `hi`, not `lo`.** The right end is a reliable reference: comparing `mid` with `hi` tells you which side the drop is on in every case, including a list that was not rotated at all. Comparing with `lo` is ambiguous when the whole list is in order.

**Mind the bounds.** When `nums[mid] <= nums[hi]`, `mid` itself may be the minimum, so keep it: `hi = mid`, not `mid - 1`, and loop while `lo < hi`. The loop ends with `lo == hi` on the minimum.

**Complexity.** O(log n) time, O(1) space.

**Follow-up.** With duplicates, `nums[mid] == nums[hi]` tells you nothing about the side. Shrinking `hi` by one is safe, and the worst case becomes O(n).
